jsnvu6-e147544-d1e106.summary: Rubric heading for Question 4, stating the question to be treated—whether religious are bound to obey their superiors in all things—and cross-referencing the parallel treatment in Aquinas, Summa Theologiae II-II, q.104, a.5.
concepts: religious obedience
cross-reference to Aquinas ST II-II q.104 a.5

jsnvu6-e147544-d1e124.summary: Opens the treatment of religious obedience with two sub-questions: first, whether religious are bound to obey their superiors in all things; second, to whom a religious owes greater obedience—his own religious superior, or the bishop or pope.
concepts: division of the question into scope of obedience and hierarchy of obedience

jsnvu6-e147544-d1e138.summary: First objection (arguing for unlimited obedience): among ordered things, the first relates to the second as the second relates to the third; among subject, prelate, and God there is an order of prelacy and subjection such that the prelate is a mean between subject and God; therefore, just as the prelate is bound to obey God, so the subject is bound to obey the prelate; but the prelate is bound to obey God in all things; therefore the subject is likewise bound to obey the prelate in all things.
claims: Ordered relations transfer proportionally: as prelate is to God, so subject is to prelate
The prelate must obey God in all things
Therefore, by the same proportion, the subject must obey the prelate in all things
concepts: proportional order of subject-prelate-God
argument from analogous obligation

jsnvu6-e147544-d1e153.summary: Second objection: just as a religious, in professing, vows chastity and poverty, so too obedience; but a religious is bound to keep chastity and poverty in all things; therefore he is likewise bound to obedience in all things.
claims: The three vows (chastity, poverty, obedience) are professed together
Chastity and poverty bind without limitation
Therefore obedience should likewise bind without limitation
concepts: parity argument among the three religious vows

jsnvu6-e147544-d1e165.summary: Sed contra: Bernard (De Praecepto et Dispensatione I) says a subject is not to be compelled beyond what he has promised; but no religious promises to obey in all things; therefore religious are not bound to obey their superiors in all things.
claims: Bernard holds that obligation does not exceed what was actually promised
No religious vow promises obedience in all things
Therefore religious are not bound to unlimited obedience
concepts: Bernard on the limits of promised obligation

jsnvu6-e147544-d1e176.summary: Responsio: the obedience owed by religious arises from their vow of religion, since only by vow does one obligate oneself beyond the common obligation necessary for salvation owed by everyone; but the vow of religion is not a vow to obey in all things—no religious profession has this form—but rather to obey according to the rule and the legitimate statutes of the order. Therefore no religious is bound to obey his superior in all things, but only in what is expressed in the rule and the order's statutes, or reducible to them.
claims: The obedience owed by religious is grounded specifically in the vow of religion, which exceeds the common obligation owed by all Christians
The vow of religion binds obedience only to the rule and legitimate statutes of the order, not to unlimited commands
Religious are bound to obey their superior only in matters expressed in, or reducible to, the rule and statutes
concepts: vow of religion as the source and measure of obedience
obedience limited to the rule and statutes

jsnvu6-e147544-d1e200.summary: Specifies the two kinds of matters reducible to the vow of religion: some are reducible by way of presupposition, such as the precepts of natural and divine law, which the vows of religious presuppose—hence religious can be punished by their superiors not only for transgressing the counsels they vowed but also for transgressing precepts (theft, adultery, perjury, blasphemy, and the like), unless punishment of such crimes is reserved to higher authorities. Others are reducible by way of consequence, such as matters of mutual service and similar things without which the good state of religious life could not be maintained. These two kinds are the matters in which a religious is bound to obey his superior, being contained in the vow of profession either expressly or by reduction; in other matters he is not bound to obey. Bernard is cited: let the prelate forbid me nothing of what I promised, and require nothing more than I promised; obeying commands that are merely licit is good, and constitutes obedience that is not strictly necessary but 'perfect'; but obeying in all things, even illicit ones, is foolish, constituting rash obedience.
claims: Matters binding a religious's obedience fall into two classes: those reducible by presupposition (natural and divine precepts, already binding independently of the vow) and those reducible by consequence (mutual services necessary for the order's good functioning)
A religious can be punished by his superior for violating precepts as well as counsels, unless punishment is reserved to higher authority
Per Bernard, obedience to licit commands beyond strict necessity is 'perfect' obedience, while obedience extended to illicit commands is foolish and rash, not virtuous
concepts: reducibility by presupposition versus by consequence
precepts versus counsels
Bernard's distinction between perfect and rash obedience

jsnvu6-e147544-d1e244.summary: Reply to the first argument (d1e138): prelates are intermediaries between God and the people not with respect to all things, but only with respect to what pertains to the right of their prelacy, and in these matters they are to be obeyed as standing in God's place, per Luke 10 ('he who hears you hears me')—but not in absolutely all things.
claims: The prelate's mediating role between God and the people is limited to the scope of his proper prelacy, not unlimited
Obedience owed to the prelate as standing in God's place (Luke 10) is correspondingly limited to that scope
concepts: reply to objection
scope-limited mediation of the prelate
Luke 10 on hearing the prelate as hearing God

jsnvu6-e147544-d1e260.summary: Reply to the second argument (d1e153): chastity and poverty have a determinate subject matter around which they are exercised, not limited within the profession of religion itself; obedience, by contrast, has the broadest possible subject matter, since anything licit could in principle fall under a vow of obedience—but because many licit things would contribute nothing to the perfection of religious life, the vow of obedience is limited, in each order, to certain definite matters better suited to the order's proximate end, which end varies among different religious orders.
claims: Chastity and poverty have a fixed, determinate scope that does not depend on the profession, unlike obedience, whose potential scope is unlimited
Because obedience's potential scope is unlimited, each religious order limits its vow of obedience to matters suited to its own particular proximate end, which varies by order
concepts: reply to objection
fixed scope of chastity/poverty versus unlimited potential scope of obedience
variation of proximate ends among religious orders

jsnvu6-e147544.summary: Question 4 asks whether religious are bound to obey their superiors in all things. Objections argue from the proportional order of subject-prelate-God (as the prelate obeys God in all things, so the subject should obey the prelate in all things) and from parity with the unlimited vows of chastity and poverty; the sed contra invokes Bernard's principle that obligation does not exceed what was actually promised, and no religious promises unlimited obedience. The responsio grounds religious obedience specifically in the vow of religion, which binds only to the rule and legitimate statutes of the order—not to everything a superior might command—distinguishing matters reducible to the vow by presupposition (natural and divine precepts, independently binding) from those reducible by consequence (mutual services necessary to the order's good functioning), and citing Bernard's distinction between 'perfect' obedience to licit commands and foolish, 'rash' obedience extended to illicit ones. The replies to the opening objections clarify that the prelate's mediating role between God and the people, and hence the obedience owed him, is limited to the scope of his proper office (Luke 10), and that obedience differs from chastity and poverty in having an unlimited potential scope, which each order therefore must deliberately limit to matters suited to its own particular end.
claims: Religious obedience is grounded in and measured by the vow of religion, binding only to the rule and legitimate statutes of the order, not to a superior's commands without limit

Obedience extends to natural and divine precepts (presupposed by the vow) and to matters of mutual service necessary for the order's good functioning, but not beyond what is expressed or reducible to the vow
Obedience to licit commands beyond strict necessity is virtuous ('perfect') obedience; obedience extended to illicit commands is foolish and rash, not virtuous

Obedience's potential scope is unlimited (unlike chastity and poverty's fixed scope), which is precisely why each order must deliberately limit its vow of obedience to matters suited to its own particular end
concepts: religious obedience grounded in the vow
precepts versus counsels
reducibility by presupposition versus consequence
Bernard on perfect versus rash obedience
variable proximate ends of religious orders
